extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, third-party requesters, and patent practitioners considering or handling USPTO ex parte reexamination
extracted.subtask_short: ex parte reexamination filing and review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on filing and prosecuting USPTO ex parte reexamination requests: eligibility, permissible grounds (patents/printed publications only), the Central Reexamination Unit's initial "substantial new question of patentability" determination, prosecution flow, limitations, costs, and strategic considerations versus other post-grant mechanisms or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to file
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may, at any time during the period of enforceability of a patent, file a request for ex parte reexamination. Requests may be filed by the patent owner or by third-party requesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes broad standing ("any person") and that both patent owners and third parties can initiate the process. Timing is limited to the patent's enforceability period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds (prior art limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexamination is based only on prior art patents or printed publications — i.e., grounds under §102 and §103. Challenges under §101 or §112 are not permitted in ex parte reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only patents and printed publications may be relied upon in the request; statutory questions (subject matter eligibility) and written-description/enablement issues (§101/§112) are outside the scope of ex parte reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ) threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office initially determines whether the request presents a "substantial new question of patentability." If a substantial new question is presented, reexamination is ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SNQ is the threshold for instituting reexamination. Even prior art that was previously considered can present a new question if viewed differently. The patent owner has the opportunity to contest the substantiality of the new question during the initial determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination procedural flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical procedure: (1) Request filed by patent owner or third party; (2) Initial determination by the Central Reexamination Unit (CRU); (3) If granted, reexamination proceeds; (4) Patent owner statement allowed (optional); (5) Office actions issue similar to regular prosecution; (6) Patent owner response required; (7) Reexamination certificate issued (cancels, amends, or confirms claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prosecution during reexamination resembles normal examiner–applicant interactions after institution, culminating in a reexamination certificate that resolves the claims' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party participation limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although members of the public may initiate ex parte reexaminations, once the request is submitted they no longer actively participate; subsequent correspondence is strictly between the examiner and the patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limited participation means third parties cannot engage in continued adversarial prosecution (no ongoing filings or direct correspondence) — contrast with inter partes or IPR-type proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and substantive limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexamination has several limitations: no discovery, no oral hearing, cannot challenge §101 or §112 issues, and grounds are limited to patents/printed publications (§102/§103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these limits, ex parte reexamination is less adversarial and narrower in scope than other post-grant proceedings; patent owners can also amend claims during prosecution (often used to escape narrow grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and fee considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing fees and overall cost are generally lower than some other post-grant proceedings: ex parte reexamination filing fee approximately $12,000 (USPTO) for a standard request, compared with IPR (approximately $19,000–$41,500 with institution fees) and PGR (around $30,000+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost comparisons are provided to help petitioners choose between reexamination, IPR, and PGR based on budget and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: When to consider filing ex parte reexamination: limited budget for invalidation challenge; when a patent owner does not want claims broadened; to avoid a fully adversarial proceeding; after the IPR window has closed; when the available prior art consists of patents or printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the goal is complete invalidation or merely narrowing scope, and consider timing relative to litigation and other post-grant options. The narrow scope and limited third-party role may favor ex parte reexamination in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with litigation and estoppel effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte reexamination can run in parallel with district court litigation. Courts may stay litigation pending reexamination, and USPTO findings can affect litigation. Statutory estoppel from reexamination is limited compared to IPR estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should consider the potential for stays and how USPTO decisions might be used in court; the estoppel consequences differ materially from AIA post-grant proceedings like IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filing recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: file reexamination early, provide the best prior art with detailed explanations, and consider whether your goal is invalidation or scope reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early filing and well-supported submissions increase chances of institution and effective prosecution. Detailed explanations help the CRU/examiner understand why the cited patents/printed publications create a substantial new question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes of reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: A reexamination certificate is issued at the conclusion, which may cancel claims, amend claims, or confirm claims as patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that outcome can either eliminate claims, narrow them via amendment, or leave them intact; amendments during reexamination can affect subsequent enforceability and validity considerations.
